analysis.one_liner: Requires drugmakers to pay Medicare rebates and lets Medicare negotiate Part B drug prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a retiring senator with no cosponsors in October 2011, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced prescription drug manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare on drugs billed under Medicare Part B (doctor-administered drugs like chemotherapy), and required the government to negotiate prices directly with manufacturers for drugs where Medicare buys most of the units. It would have paid both drugs at the cheaper price when two drugs do the same job, imposed disclosure and fiduciary duties on pharmacy benefit managers, and expanded the 340B drug discount program to PACE plans serving frail seniors. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would face lower cost-sharing on expensive Part B drugs, and taxpayers, who fund Medicare and would save through rebates, negotiated prices, and least-costly-alternative payments. Safety-net PACE programs would gain access to 340B discounted drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate on Part B drugs, modeled on the Medicaid rebate system including an inflation penalty, so the government recoups money when prices rise faster than inflation [S2][S3].
Directs the HHS Secretary to negotiate prices with manufacturers for any drug where Medicare Part B is the majority purchaser, rather than paying an average of manufacturer-set prices [S2][S3].
Pays functionally equivalent drugs at the rate of the least costly alternative, so Medicare stops paying more for a drug that does the same job as a cheaper one [S2][S3].

Imposes fiduciary duties on pharmacy benefit managers contracting with federal health programs, requiring them to disclose when they substitute a more expensive drug, pass through payments for promoting costlier drugs, and reveal all financial arrangements with drug companies [S2][S3].

Adds PACE programs for frail elderly people to the 340B drug discount program, and lets organizations offering drug coverage keep 10% of estimated federal savings from the discount program if they spend it on enhanced coverage or health IT [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Part B revenues would be cut by rebates and negotiated prices, and pharmacy benefit managers, who would have to pass through and disclose payments they currently keep. Physicians who buy drugs and bill Medicare (such as oncology practices) would face scrutiny of the 6% markup they earn on drug purchases.

drawbacks.text: Paying functionally equivalent drugs at the least costly alternative rate can reduce access to newer, better-tolerated therapies if the government's definition of 'functionally equivalent' is too broad; a similar Medicare policy for chemotherapy drugs drew objections on these grounds.

Rebates and price negotiation would cut manufacturer revenue on Part B drugs, and opponents argue that revenue funds research into new therapies; the bill also adds administrative burden, including a new certification form for off-label antipsychotic prescribing in nursing homes.
The 10% savings bonus paid to Part D plans that join the 340B program is an additional federal cost, and its estimated-savings formula would depend on regulations yet to be written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main provisions — Part B rebates, negotiation, and PBM transparency — are large, well-defined savings to Medicare and its beneficiaries, and Part B drugs are among the most expensive in the program. The access risks from least-costly-alternative payment are real but manageable if the Secretary defines equivalence carefully, and the PBM disclosure rules address middleman payments that today are largely invisible to the agencies paying the bills. On balance the costs fall on drug makers and intermediaries, not patients, though the bill's complexity and the unknown size of the savings bonus are legitimate design concerns.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in October 2011, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Herb Kohl introduced the Prescription Drug Cost Reduction Act in the Senate on October 12, 2011 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 112th Congress [S5].

The bill would have required manufacturer rebates on Medicare Part B drugs, direct price negotiation where Medicare is the majority buyer, and payment at the least costly alternative for functionally equivalent drugs [S2][S3].
It would also have imposed fiduciary and disclosure duties on pharmacy benefit managers contracting with federal health programs [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers kept the existing system, in which Medicare pays benchmark prices set off manufacturer list prices for Part B drugs and PBM payments are not disclosed to federal agencies. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers continue to pay the higher prices the bill targeted.

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 12, 2011; it was his only action on it before retiring at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee and he never scheduled a hearing or markup; the complete action record shows nothing after the referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their lobby
against.what_they_did: The industry broadly opposed Medicare negotiation and Part B rebate proposals during this period; no industry opposition activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no party split is visible in the record; a Democrat sponsored it and a Democratic committee chair declined to move it.

industries.note: The bill required manufacturers to pay Medicare rebates on Part B drugs, to negotiate prices where Medicare is the majority purchaser, and to accept least-costly-alternative payment — direct cuts to revenue on some of the most expensive drugs Medicare buys. Those savings would have flowed to the program and to beneficiaries' lower cost-sharing.

The bill made PBMs fiduciaries of federal agencies and forced disclosure of payments they receive for promoting or substituting more expensive drugs, including rebates they currently keep rather than pass through. The bill targeted exactly the opaque middleman payments that let intermediaries profit at the plan's expense.

industries.industry: Physicians who buy and bill Part B drugs (e.g., oncology practices)
industries.note: The bill ordered a study of the 6% markup physicians earn over a drug's purchase price and of how often they pick costlier drugs over cheaper equivalents, pointing toward removing price-based prescribing incentives. It imposed no immediate change, so the effect during the bill's life was only scrutiny.

The bill let PACE programs for frail elderly patients buy drugs at 340B discounts and gave Part D plans a share of estimated federal savings if they spent it on enhanced coverage or health IT. This lowers drug costs for vulnerable enrollees.
